stops.name: Shadiyakh, Mantiq al-Tayr — the Simurgh is themselves
stops.campa: Of the thousands who set out, only thirty birds survive the seven valleys, Quest, Love, Knowledge, Detachment, Unity, Bewilderment and Annihilation, to stand at last, stripped of everything, before the court of the Simurgh. There is no king waiting. In the mirror-bright hall they find only their own thirty reflections, and understand, all together, the pun the Persian language has carried the whole poem toward: si morgh, thirty birds, is the Simurgh's own name. The king they crossed the world to find was never separate from the finding; the annihilation of the self and the arrival at God turn out, in the end, to be the same door.
stops.quote: And all who come before My splendour see / Themselves, their own unique reality... / Though you have struggled, wandered, travelled far, / It is yourselves you see and what you are.
stops.quote_source: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds), closing verses, trans. Afkham Darbandi & Dick Davis

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Mokhtar-nama and the Pand-nama
stops.campa: In his later years Attar sets down the Mokhtar-nama, more than two thousand quatrains sorted by subject as a concordance to his own thought, and the small, plain-spoken Pand-nama, the Book of Counsel, couplets of household and devotional advice simple enough that generations of Persian schoolchildren after him will learn their letters from its lines. Beside the towering ambition of the birds and their king, these are modest books, but they carry his voice into rooms the mathnavis never reach: the kitchen, the primer, the cheap copied pamphlet sold beside the mosque door for a coin.

stops.name: Nishapur, blessed by Attar
stops.campa: An old man now, more than seventy years into a life that began before the Seljuks fell, Attar receives at Nishapur a scholar fleeing west out of Balkh with his household, ahead of a horror gathering in the east that Attar can already half-name. He watches the father walk ahead and the small son trail after, and says, to those standing near, the sentence tradition will not let go: here comes a sea followed by an ocean. He calls the boy to him, puts into his hands his own Asrar-nama, and tells the bystanders this child will soon set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers.
stops.quote: Here comes a sea followed by an ocean.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Farid al-Din Attar on receiving the family of Baha al-Din Valad at Nishapur (Dowlatshah, Tadhkirat al-Shu'ara; Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, news of Otrar
stops.campa: Word reaches Nishapur's caravanserais, a season late as such word always is, of an outrage the year before at the frontier town of Otrar: a trade caravan sent by the Mongol khan Genghis seized on the governor's order, its merchants killed as spies, its goods taken. Traders passing through Attar's own city shake their heads over it as one more of the frontier's usual quarrels, a Sultan's officer overreaching, nothing that need trouble Khorasan's cities deep in the interior. Attar, past seventy now, has outlived enough fires and earthquakes to distrust anyone's certainty that a distant spark will stay distant.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, news of Bukhara and Samarkand
stops.campa: Within two years the frontier quarrel has become an empire's ruin: refugees stumbling into Nishapur from the north report Bukhara's great mosque turned into a stable for Mongol horses and its citizens driven before the army as living shields, then Samarkand's citadel, the Sultan's own capital, fallen after the shortest of resistances. Attar, who once walked the roads these very refugees are now fleeing down, listens to their accounts with the attention of a man who has spent a life collecting the last words of the dying. He does not yet know that Khorasan, and his own city, stand next in the line of march.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, submission to Jebe and Subutai
stops.campa: In May the vanguard of the Mongol advance, under the generals Jebe and Subutai, arrives before Nishapur itself demanding provisions for their march onward toward the fleeing Sultan. The city's council, weighing the fate of Bukhara and Samarkand, opens its gates and supplies what is asked rather than test its walls against the army that has taken both; the generals accept the tribute and ride on in June, leaving Nishapur standing, spared by its own quick submission. Attar, who has seen his city rebuilt once from fire and once from earthquake, watches this newest storm pass by at a distance and, for the moment, without blood.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, Toquchar slain beneath the walls
stops.campa: The peace does not hold. Through the summer, rumors run through Nishapur that the Mongols have been beaten back elsewhere, and the city, encouraged past its own safety, turns on the small occupying garrison left to enforce the khan's writ. In November, Toquchar, son-in-law to Genghis Khan himself, rides up to put down the trouble in person and takes an arrow from the wall for his trouble, dying of the wound before his own camp. Word of a khan's son-in-law killed by Nishapur's own defenders travels back along the Mongol lines faster than any caravan ever carried silk, and it travels with only one possible answer attached to it.

stops.name: Nishapur, the siege of Tolui, three pyramids of skulls
stops.campa: In April, Tolui, Genghis Khan's own son, brings the full weight of a Mongol army against the walls his brother-in-law died beneath, and Toquchar's widow is given the city to do with as she wills. The town that once bought peace with tribute is shown no second mercy: the walls are breached in seventy places, the population put to the sword down to the cats and dogs, the chroniclers say, and the skulls of men, women and children stacked in three separate pyramids. Attar, past seventy-five and still in the city by every report, is among the multitude within the walls when the gates give way.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the ransom refused
stops.campa: Among the dead and the doomed of the sack, tradition places one particular scene: an old man taken captive by a Mongol soldier, worth something alive to whoever can sell him on. A passerby offers a thousand pieces of silver, and the captor hesitates over the price. It is Attar himself, the story insists, who tells his own captor not to sell so cheap, that a better offer will come. Then another passerby offers a sack of straw, and Attar tells the soldier to take that price instead, for that is exactly what he is worth. Enraged at the silver he has lost, the Mongol kills him where he stands.
stops.quote: Don't sell me as cheaply; you will find someone willing to give more... Sell me to him, for that is all I am worth.
stops.quote_source: Legend of Attar's death in the sack of Nishapur, April 1221, as given in New World Encyclopedia, 'Farid ad-Din Attar' (after Margaret Smith)
